summaries.headline: OpenAI Expands ChatGPT Research Grants, Shares Usage Data
summaries.summary: OpenAI will offer 50,000 new ChatGPT for Academic Researchers grants starting November 23, extending Plus-level access to as many as 150,000 researchers and doubling the program's overall reach to 200,000 scientists worldwide. A companion study of the summer pilot, drawn from 580,186 messages and a survey of 251 scientists, found participants estimated their work would have taken about 1.9 times as long without AI, with coding tasks showing the largest reported gains at 2.83 times and checking or correcting outputs cited as the most common difficulty. For education leaders tracking AI's trajectory in research and instruction, the findings reinforce a now-familiar pattern: meaningful time savings paired with an unresolved verification burden that falls back on the human user.

summaries.headline: UNESCO Offers Framework for Teaching AI Literacy
summaries.summary: UNESCO has released a teaching guide designed to help educators prepare students to critically evaluate AI-generated text, images, audio and video, and to understand the algorithms shaping what they see online. The resource, a companion to UNESCO's 2021 media literacy curriculum already piloted in more than 40 countries, organizes material around five areas including AI in everyday life, algorithmic bias and human rights, and was developed with eight international experts and peer-reviewed by ten more. As AI-mediated information becomes routine for students, the guide gives curriculum developers and teacher-training programs a ready-made framework rather than requiring them to build critical-thinking instruction around AI from scratch.

summaries.headline: West Virginia Officials Move to Kill Funding Suit
summaries.summary: West Virginia Attorney General John McCuskey and legislative leaders filed a motion on Nov. 13 asking the state Supreme Court to dismiss a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the state's school funding formula, arguing the court lacks jurisdiction and that House Speaker Roger Hanshaw and Senate President Randy Smith are protected by legislative immunity. The suit, brought in September by a Lincoln County sixth-grader through the ACLU of West Virginia, names 29 state and local officials and entities as respondents, and state attorneys separately contend the petitioner failed to establish standing by not tying alleged harm to specific actions by officials like the state auditor or treasurer. The dismissal push comes just days after the Department of Education and state board backed holding the case in abeyance while they pursue draft legislation — approved Oct. 14 — to revise the school aid formula ahead of the 2027 legislative session, signaling officials prefer a legislative fix over judicial intervention.

summaries.headline: Texas Bill Would Fund Schools on Enrollment, Not Attendance
summaries.summary: Texas Rep. John Bucy has filed House Bill 376 to shift school funding from daily attendance counts to total enrollment, a change that would bring Texas in line with 45 states already using that model. The bill lands as South San Antonio ISD weighs closing five campuses and cutting staff after a local funding proposition failed, with closures estimated to save about $6 million, while a speaker at a nearby North East ISD meeting suggested new state funding might not arrive until June 2027. The gap between a district's immediate budget pressures and the legislature's timeline leaves families and school boards making consequential decisions well before lawmakers settle the funding question.

summaries.headline: New Study Finds Modest Gains From Phone Bans
summaries.summary: A new Harvard and Dartmouth study of 3.3 million students across 4,600 schools finds that strict cell phone bans using locked Yondr pouches produce small but steady test score gains, roughly equivalent to one to two extra weeks of instruction per year. The effect size, about 0.01 standard deviations annually, is tiny by conventional standards but researchers note it mirrors about half the magnitude of pre-pandemic annual test score declines, and gains held steady across elementary, middle, and high schools regardless of poverty level or achievement — though lower-performing students saw no extra boost. The findings complicate an earlier national study that found "close to zero" effect on scores, with one researcher involved in that work calling the new results "sobering" and cautioning against projecting that small annual gains will compound, even as study author Tom Kane argues that at $25 to $30 per student, pouches are a low-cost bet compared to interventions like tutoring.

summaries.headline: Enrollment Falls, But Staffing Doesn't
summaries.summary: District leaders nationwide are holding onto school buildings and staff even as student populations shrink, with a new Stanford study finding that one in four public schools has lost 15 percent or more of its enrollment since 2019 while teacher headcounts have actually grown by 1 percent nationally. Seattle exemplifies the pattern: enrollment has dropped roughly 8 percent since 2019 to below 49,000 students, yet proposals to close campuses have repeatedly collapsed under community pressure, including a 2024 plan to shutter a fifth of schools. With pandemic relief funds now exhausted and research from Arkansas, California and Chicago showing closures yield only modest, temporary savings, districts face a structural budget problem that building closures alone won't solve — leaving the harder question, as one Seattle board member put it, of how to serve students well with fewer resources.

summaries.headline: Mississippi Mandates a Preschool Math Curriculum
summaries.summary: Mississippi has become the first state to require a specific math curriculum, Building Blocks, across its state-funded pre-K programs, which currently serve roughly 8,700 children, or about a quarter of the state's four-year-olds. Rolled out since 2022 with full implementation expected by August 2027, the curriculum emphasizes hands-on, language-rich instruction — like distinguishing a rhombus's straight sides and angles — over worksheets or basic counting drills, addressing what University of Michigan researcher Christina Weiland calls a widespread tendency for preschools to neglect math or treat it superficially. The state hopes the effort, backed by the University of Michigan's Education Policy Initiative, can replicate the momentum of its literacy gains, with state officials betting that standardizing curriculum and coaching statewide can close a similar gap in early math achievement.

summaries.headline: Denver Board, Superintendent Clash Over Goal-Setting
summaries.summary: Denver Public Schools Superintendent Alex Marrero and his school board are at odds over whether his academic targets are ambitious enough, stalling board approval of goals that also serve as his performance evaluation. Marrero's math proficiency target for Latino students is 21%, just over 2 percentage points above last year, and his districtwide reading target for grades three through eight is 43%, prompting board Vice President Monica Hunter to question approving a goal that leaves nearly 80% of students short of proficiency; Marrero counters that steeper targets would require reallocating hundreds of thousands of dollars away from higher-performing, whiter and wealthier schools. The standoff echoes a years-long debate in Denver over aspirational versus realistic goal-setting, dating back to predecessor Tom Boasberg's unmet 80%-proficiency target, and reflects a broader governance rift that has left board members unable to even agree on scheduling a vote.

summaries.headline: Denver Board Narrows Vacancy Field to Three
summaries.summary: The Denver school board has narrowed 12 applicants for a vacant District 3 seat down to three finalists: former board candidate Caron Blanke, Chinook Fund program manager P. Barclay Jones, and former DPS administrator Verónica Figoli Fleischer. The vacancy, created by DJ Torres's resignation amid policy-violation accusations, comes as the board navigates visible tension with Superintendent Alex Marrero and internal infighting, with board President Xóchitl Gaytán publicly ruling out candidates she ties to "dark money" influence and criticism of the superintendent. The board will interview each finalist for 20 minutes on Thursday and must fill the seat by November 29, a decision that will shape the board's fragile balance of power heading into 2027.

summaries.headline: Oregon Attendance Ticks Up, Gaps Remain Wide
summaries.summary: Oregon's regular school attendance rate climbed a percentage point to 68% in 2025-26, with state officials citing gains in early elementary grades as evidence that targeted efforts are working, even as the rate stays below pre-pandemic levels and among the lowest in the nation. In Salem-Keizer Public Schools, 42% of students were chronically absent, with stark demographic splits: 36.4% of white students missed significant school time compared to 60.8% of Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander students and 73% of homeless students, while the district's largest high school, McKay, saw only 36% of students attending regularly. State officials and district spokespeople point to belonging and community partnership as levers for progress, but the persistent gaps across race, poverty, and homelessness status suggest attendance recovery is uneven at best — and that the students most affected by instability outside school are also the hardest to bring back inside it.

summaries.headline: Delhi Rolls Out Districtwide Student Mental Health Policy
summaries.summary: The Delhi government has launched a Mental Well-Being Policy covering children and young people up to 29 years old, including those outside the formal education system, with a proposed staffing ratio of one counsellor per 500 school students and one per 100 higher-education students. The policy brings roughly 23 lakh school students under a common support system — about 15 lakh in Directorate of Education-run schools and 8 lakh in private schools — and follows a two-stage model starting with mental health assessments before counselling referrals, backed by handbooks that train teachers, administrative, and transport staff to spot early signs of distress. Developed with input from NITI Aayog, UNESCO, and INMAS, the policy signals a shift toward treating emotional wellness as infrastructure that spans beyond the classroom to every adult a student encounters in a school day.

summaries.headline: $1.05M Funds AI Pilots for Multilingual Classrooms
summaries.summary: Multilingual by Design has awarded $350,000 each to three teams building AI tools that help teachers track multilingual students' classroom discussions and adapt instructional materials to their language needs, with pilots launching in 2026-27 across Wisconsin, Massachusetts and Colorado. The projects target distinct classroom needs: a University of Wisconsin-Madison tool will give teachers real-time insight into small-group math discussions even when they don't share a student's first language, a Joan Ganz Cooney Center and Medley Learning project will help Taunton teachers adapt existing materials with shorter text and embedded definitions, and a DSST Public Schools tool will help Denver and Aurora teachers align math lessons with English language development frameworks across a network where more than 65% of students are current or former multilingual learners. With NCES data showing 67.3% of public school teachers instruct at least one English learner, and Throughline Learning leading research across all three sites to track both classroom use and student outcomes, the pilots offer an early test of whether AI can meaningfully ease the planning burden without displacing teacher judgment.

summaries.headline: Google Expands Free AI Access for Scientists
summaries.summary: Google DeepMind has added Gemini 4 Carbon to its scientist access program, giving researchers six months of free use through Google Antigravity alongside the model's existing Argon offering, with the broader program aimed at reaching 10,000 scientists on a rolling weekly selection basis. Google reports Carbon handling complex reasoning tasks, including a protein-sequence retrieval experiment that increased related sequence matches by an average of 40 times across seven protein families, as well as cybersecurity applications where partners identified vulnerabilities in major software platforms in under two hours

summaries.headline: Ohio State, Microsoft Ink Five-Year AI Partnership
summaries.summary: Ohio State and Microsoft have launched a five-year partnership combining AI training and certification access for students, employees and Ohio communities with a major overhaul of the university's healthcare and research technology infrastructure. The deal includes moving roughly 70% to 80% of Ohio State's storage and computing to Microsoft Azure, a new Fabric and OneLake data platform meant to connect clinical and research information across the medical center and campuses, and clinician use of Dragon Copilot's ambient note-drafting tool, though no workload-savings figures have been released. While K-12 districts aren't direct partners here, the deal signals how higher-ed and health systems are structuring large-scale AI workforce pipelines and data infrastructure that could eventually shape regional talent pathways and expectations for AI fluency.

summaries.headline: State Officials Move to Dismiss Funding Suit
summaries.summary: The West Virginia Attorney General's Office filed a motion last week to dismiss a lawsuit from an ACLU-West Virginia-backed petitioner seeking a court order forcing the Legislature to overhaul the state's school funding system under the constitution's "thorough and efficient" clause. State lawyers argue legislative immunity shields the Speaker of the House and Senate President from suit over statute-making decisions, and that the petitioner — a sixth-grader from Lincoln County — hasn't established standing through direct harm or verified taxpayer status. The filing lands as the state grapples with special education cost deficits, a drop of more than 8,000 students statewide, and warnings that up to 20 schools could face closure or consolidation, underscoring how deeply the funding fight is tied to the system's current strain rather than an abstract legal question.

summaries.headline: Sherrill Warns Next Budget Could Strain School Funding
summaries.summary: Gov. Mikie Sherrill told local leaders at the New Jersey League of Municipalities conference that her second state budget, due June 30, 2027, could prove tougher than the $60.7 billion plan she signed this past June, citing uncertainty from federal cuts under the Trump administration. She reaffirmed plans to overhaul the state's long-criticized school funding formula and to bring stakeholders together on soaring public-worker health benefit costs, both of which hit local government budgets hardest since municipalities shoulder major shares of school and employee health expenses. With no new policy details offered and committees still weighing solutions, district and municipal leaders face continued uncertainty over funding formulas and benefit costs that could translate into staff cuts, service reductions, or property tax hikes.

summaries.headline: Missouri Delays School Funding Overhaul Until 2027
summaries.summary: A Missouri task force that spent nearly 18 months studying an overhaul of the state's school funding formula will withhold its recommendations until July 2027, after state Sen. Rusty Black cited looming budget cuts and property tax reduction proposals as reasons to delay. The group's proposed changes would increase the formula's cost by more than $600 million, even as the current formula is already projected to be underfunded by roughly $300 million next fiscal year, and lawmakers now face cutting $1.5 to $3.5 billion from agency budget requests. The report remains unreleased to the public, drawing criticism from Democratic lawmakers who question whether the task force's call for increased funding — rather than the flat funding Gov. Mike Kehoe initially requested — is the real reason behind the delay.

summaries.headline: Delhi Mandates School Counsellors Amid Student Suicide Crisis
summaries.summary: Delhi has launched Ehsaas, a mental health and well-being policy that calls for one counsellor for every 500 school students and one for every 100 higher education students, making it the first city in India to adopt such a framework. The policy responds to NCRB data showing 1,284 suicide deaths among children under 18 in Delhi between 2017 and 2021, an average of 257 children a year, or roughly five deaths weekly. Psychiatrists note the policy's impact hinges on consistent follow-up and training counsellors to spot early warning signs, while stigma and lack of awareness among students, parents, and teachers remain barriers to students speaking up in the first place.

summaries.headline: College Study Maps Four Distinct Distress Trajectories
summaries.summary: A year-long study of 458 students at a German university tracked psychological distress monthly using the Depression, Anxiety, Stress Scale and identified four distinct trajectories: low distress (36.9%), moderate distress (32.1%), moderate-high distress (23.8%), and high distress (7.2%), with the high-distress group remaining persistently elevated while the other three groups saw declines over the year. summaries.headline: Microsoft Pushes Standards for Auditing AI Agents
summaries.summary: Microsoft has launched an AI Transparency Initiative with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to build common standards for tracking what AI agents do, what data they access and whether their actions match system records. The effort responds to a growing blind spot as agents take on recurring, multi-step tasks: organizations may know what was requested and what resulted, but have no reliable way to verify what happened in between, or to trace authorization and evidence across different models and providers. For district IT and compliance teams weighing AI agents for administrative or instructional workflows, this signals that auditability — not just capability — is becoming a baseline expectation, with Microsoft planning to build the resulting evidence trail directly into Copilot, Foundry and its broader AI stack.

local_articles.summary: Looming budget cuts lead school funding task force to delay report  Springfield Daily Citizen

![](https://i0.wp.com/sgfcitizen.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/050826_spsTOTY_EF_102.jpg?fit=780%2C482&ssl=1)Springfield Public Schools students practiced telling time in Spanish using adjustable clocks on a Friday morning late in the school year. (Photo by Ellie Frysztak)

![Everlit Audio Player](https://i0.wp.com/sgfcitizen.org/wp-content/plugins/everlit/images/player-standard.jpg?w=780&ssl=1)

Subscribe today to listen to this content [Get Access](https://sgfcitizen.org/schools/k12-education/task-force-delays-funding-formula/)

Uncertainty over funding Missouri’s public schools and how lawmakers will tackle that problem during the upcoming session, has led to a delay in delivering a report aimed at improving how those schools are funded.

The [Missouri School Funding Modernization Task Force](https://dese.mo.gov/financial-admin-services/school-finance/missouri-school-funding-modernization-task-force-executive-order-25-14) was assembled at the order of Gov. Mike Kehoe and tasked with delivering a report by Dec. 1.

During the ad hoc committee’s most recent meeting, held Monday, Nov. 16, in Jefferson City, its chair recommended waiting to deliver that final report until after the General Assembly’s next legislative session — likely in July, said [committee member Tom Prater.](https://sgfcitizen.org/schools/k12-education/now-off-state-board-tom-prater-named-to-school-funding-task-force/) Sen. Rusty Black, R-Chillicothe, is chair of the task force. Prater was appointed to the committee in 2025 by Kehoe.

Prater said that the reasoning makes sense, given recent funding reductions that schools are already facing. The committee has been at work for almost two years in anticipation of the Dec. 1 deadline.

“Our initial intent was to have a report containing two options for a new funding formula,” Prater said in an interview Monday after the meeting. “But over two years, the budget and the situation in the state has changed, and caused some angst everywhere in Jefferson City.”

![](https://i0.wp.com/sgfcitizen.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/041625_prater1-1536x922-1.jpg?resize=780%2C468&ssl=1)Tom Prater, an eye surgeon from Springfield, listens to questions about his time on Springfield Public Schools’ board during the Senate Gubernatorial Appointments Committee hearing. (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent)

Kehoe’s office confirmed the delay and accepted it, based on the upcoming legislative session, where ideas such as property tax reform and deeper budget cuts will be considered. According to a prepared statement sent to the Daily Citizen, he thanked committee members for their time so far.

“Governor Kehoe remains committed to developing a school funding foundation formula that reflects the needs of today’s students, families, and educators, rather than those of 20 years ago, ensuring Missouri’s public education system is positioned for long-term success,” according to a statement sent by Communications Director Gabby Picard.

The committee’s delay frustrated Democrats, said Kansas City Rep. Ashley Aune, Minority Leader. In a press release, Aune said that Missourians deserve to see the plan as soon as possible, and that House Democrats would fight any effort to continue funding private school scholarships with taxpayer funds.

“The Kehoe administration’s education policy has always been to defund public schools and use taxpayer money to support private schools,” Aune said in a press release. “With the drubbing anti-public school candidates took in the recent election, it’s no wonder he’d like to hide his plan until next summer, but Missourians can’t wait.”

## Task force fixing problems with current formula

The foundation formula is an algorithm that uses statistics such as property tax rates and student attendance to distribute money across Missouri’s more than 500 school districts as fairly as possible. The formula allows the state to budget a single amount without making micro-decisions specific to each school.

Prater said that formula has a lot of problems that the task force was trying to fix — and got close to fixing. According to drafts of their work, the task force had a model that could give schools a net gain of about $600 million, and also switched a measurement of attendance to enrollment.

The draft also made progress toward equitable funding given the disparity of property tax rates between richer urban districts and poorer rural districts.

“You have some districts that are quite well off with property tax, but smaller ones are not as much,” Prater said. “Which means that the local share of the district’s funding formula may be more dependent on the state than local funding, or vice versa. That was an inequality in the way that the system was set up, and we were trying to fix that.”

Springfield, the state’s largest school district, and others in the metropolitan area would do well under such a new formula, said Prater, a former member and president of the Springfield Board of Education.

But Monday’s delay means that the legislature will rely on the old formula, which Prater called “outdated” and “antiquated.”

“There was some frustration in the room, because many of us felt like we’d done good work, and were probably close to finalizing some pilot decisions that would be good,” Prater said. “But we have to understand that political reality gets in the way. And Sen. Black told us his concern was bringing this to the governor and legislature in a time where we are uncertain about where the budget is headed.”

## Shaky future for Missouri’s schools

The delay adds to a number of developments being watched by school leaders.

Earlier this year, the General Assembly passed a budget that did not fully fund the formula. Instead of advocating for legislators to fully fund that formula, the state board [in September asked for flat funding,](https://missouriindependent.com/2026/09/15/missouri-education-board-declines-to-seek-300-million-increase-in-school-aid/) effectively turning down a $300 million increase.

At the same time, the same Legislature has invested $110 million over two years directly into MoScholars, a scholarship system that grants vouchers to parents for their students to attend qualifying private schools.

A new [A-F grading system for the state’s schools](https://sgfcitizen.org/schools/k12-education/missouri-dese-leadership-turmoil/) has also been delayed, and the State Board of Education is dealing with more turnover in leadership of the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education.

The midterm elections [brought an end to Republican supermajorities](https://sgfcitizen.org/government/elections/democrats-win-springfield-senate/) in both the House and Senate, which means Democrats will be able to offer more resistance through the legislative session.

Prater said committee members are hearing about pushback from some lawmakers. He said committee members know full well that their recommendation is subject to tweaking from lawmakers in the General Assembly.

It remains unclear if the committee will get to meet again. According to the committee’s website, Monday was the final scheduled meeting of the group. Prater said he was proud of the progress that he and his fellow committee members made.

“We really made good progress. There are a lot of smart people in that room who have a lot of knowledge about school funding,” Prater said. “We were hoping today to see some simulations of some of the products we have been working on. It didn’t get to that, but Sen. Black emphasized that we will stay in the loop, and that he wants to utilize us to finish the final product.”

_Editor’s note: Tom Prater is a member of the Springfield Daily Citizen Board of Directors. Board members are not involved in day to day news coverage decisions._

by






[Maddie Madison](https://www.newstribune.com/staff/maddie-madison)

The Missouri School Boards' Association is pushing back against a decision to delay recommendations from the Missouri School Funding Modernization Task Force until late July 2027, warning the move will sideline critical education funding decisions until after the upcoming legislative session.

In a statement released Monday, MSBA Executive Director Melissa Randol called the timeline shift "disappointing," saying it comes just weeks before lawmakers can begin prefiling bills for the next legislative session. Gov. Mike Kehoe has agreed to the delay, which task force chair Sen. Rusty Black attributed to the state's current financial circumstances.

While acknowledging Missouri's difficult budget outlook, Randol argued that financial constraints make immediate, transparent dialogue more urgent, not less.

"The task force has already completed significant work and has preliminary findings that can help to inform policymakers, educators and the public," Randol said. "We do not need to wait until July to acknowledge the realities of Missouri's school funding system or begin talking about the changes necessary to better support students and schools."

According to the MSBA, Missouri ranks near the bottom nationally in the share of public school funding provided by the state, shifting a heavier burden onto local property taxes. Randol said this dynamic creates uneven pressure on taxpayers and leads to wide disparities in student resources depending on their zip code.

The association also pointed to ongoing strain within the state's Foundation Formula, which it says is already underfunded. Recent changes have added new obligations and costs to the formula without corresponding state dollars, leaving districts uncertain about whether they will receive the resources required to meet state mandates and growing student needs.

Randol also criticized outside campaigns, such as efforts to expand gambling, that have promised hundred of millions of dollars for public education while structuring the policies so that marketing and promotional expenses absorb the bulk of early revenue.

"We should not allow public schools to be used as (a) bargaining chip at the ballot box," Randol said, calling for greater transparency and accountability regarding school funding claims.

Despite the task force's postponed deadline, the MSBA urged lawmakers and stakeholders to use existing funding data and the task force's preliminary findings to begin addressing structural school finance issues during the 2027 session rather than waiting until summer.

# Virginia School funding in for major overhaul

November 16, 2026

\|

[Daily News Headlines](https://shoredailynews.com/category/headlines/)

![Image](https://shoredailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Screenshot-2026-11-15-at-8.50.09-PM.jpg)

Accomack and Northampton County school officials are watching potential legislative action to overhaul the state’s school funding formulas.

Virginia lawmakers are taking steps toward a major overhaul of the state’s public school funding formula, a change that could impact how more than 10 billion dollars a year is distributed to school divisions across the Commonwealth.

The effort is drawing renewed attention from school leaders in Southwest and Southside Virginia, who hope a new formula will bring additional funding to small, rural school divisions and communities with larger populations of students requiring extra support.

In October, a General Assembly subcommittee approved hiring a consultant to help develop a new funding formula. The move is part of a years-long effort to replace Virginia’s current system, which has been in place for about 50 years.

[![](https://shoredailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/riverside-shore-memorial.png)](https://www.riversideonline.com/locations/hospitals/riverside-shore-memorial-hospital)

School officials say the existing formula creates significant funding differences across the state. Some school divisions spend more than twice as much per student as others.

Washington County Schools Superintendent Keith Perrigan, who also heads the Coalition of Small and Rural Schools of Virginia, has been among those pushing for changes. He says the current system does not adequately account for differences in local resources and student needs.

Virginia is one of only a handful of states that bases school funding primarily on the number of staff positions state officials determine each division needs.

Most states use student-based funding models, providing a base amount for each student, with additional money for those who need specialized services or extra assistance.

[![Alexa, enable One Oh Three the Shore Skill](https://shoredailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/103theshore-Alexa-300x250-1.jpg)](https://shoredailynews.com/alexa/)

Governor Abigail Spanberger has also pledged to modernize the funding formula and work with the General Assembly to increase state investment in public education.

The issue has gained support among lawmakers from both parties, with calls for the review to move forward quickly.

For rural school divisions like those on the Eastern Shore, the proposed changes could mean a fairer distribution of state education dollars and more resources to meet the needs of students and their communities.

Legislators and others met at the state Capitol last week as part of negotiations to find ways to refine or replace the state’s school funding formula. While much talk concerns how schools are funded, one important question must be answered before the first bill is introduced in the 2027 regular legislative session: What is the desired end result in terms of what students who receive high school diplomas should learn?

Report after report across the nation show that many students entering higher education lack basic skills that their parents had. Too many college freshmen can’t handle introductory algebra courses. Older adults sometimes are appalled at the lack of historical knowledge in young adults. That’s not the fault of young adults. It’s a deficiency in what the public education system has become. As one Marshall University professor has said, colleges cannot be expected to do in one semester what public schools failed to do in 12 years.

It’s not just West Virginia, but public schools in other states are not the West Virginia Legislature’s concern except in how our state’s public school system compares to theirs.

Blame COVID-19 shutdowns. Blame Common Core, No Child Left Behind and other programs meant to improve the education system. They’ve had successes, but they haven’t kept up with changes in the home and changes in society at large. Blame a micromanaging Legislature. Blame teacher unions. Blame President Donald Trump if you wish. The facts on the ground show that something needs to change.

Legislators could look at the Mississippi Miracle, in which decisive action by that state’s government took Mississippi schools from near the bottom in student achievement nationally to above average. The miracle relied on student accountability and financial resources, among other things. Some school districts did away with summer vacation and replaced it with longer breaks throughout the school year.

In his inauguration speech in 2025, Gov. Patrick Morrisey said his plan for education had three components: what schools children will attend, including making private schools more affordable; what students in public schools will be taught; and teacher pay. The first and third parts are measurable and are more subject to the winds of politics. The second part tends to be forgotten.

Public schools can be beneficiaries or victims of politics. Rumors that former Gov. Jim Justice, now a member of the U.S. Senate, will run for that office again in 2028 probably complicates discussions on a number of important topics, including education, leading into the 2027 session.

Parents have tried school choice. They like it, and they’re not likely to give it up voluntarily. However it adjusts the school funding formula, legislators should remember that.

Students, parents, administrators and others must be held accountable. Private schools answer to the people who pay tuition. Public schools are built to avoid accountability, and that must change.

This likely will be a process taking several years unless legislators jump in wholeheartedly and decide to repair something that is breaking down. The public school system does not need to be replaced. It needs to be competitive with the alternatives. It must win back families who have left.

# NT Daily 11/18: Business Licenses Go Online, School Funding Report Delayed & Great 8 Matchups



November 18, 2026






[https://youtu.be/QLzzIDThgXM?si=Wv-4usCRhzeIpTsf](https://youtu.be/QLzzIDThgXM?si=Wv-4usCRhzeIpTsf)

Jefferson City business owners can cross a trip to City Hall off their list. Erin Schrimpf breaks down how the city’s new online licensing system works, including what happens when you ask City Hall’s AI chatbot about a permit.

At the Capitol, the Missouri School Boards’ Association is pushing back after a school funding task force delayed its recommendations until after the 2027 legislative session.

Plus, we have updates on Tanner Bridge Road and Friday’s lane closure on Jefferson Street, a call for Christmas Bird Count volunteers, and a look at the Central Bank Great 8 Classic, where Southern Boone will make its tournament debut over Christmas break.

Join us Monday for our winter sports preview.

# Larger classes, less support? ACT parents fear school funding cuts

[Nicholas Fuller](https://canberradaily.com.au/author/nick-fuller/)

November 18, 2026

[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fcanberradaily.com.au%2Flarger-classes-less-support-act-parents-fear-school-funding-cuts%2F "Facebook") [Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Larger+classes%2C+less+support%3F+ACT+parents+fear+school+funding+cuts&url=https%3A%2F%2Fcanberradaily.com.au%2Flarger-classes-less-support-act-parents-fear-school-funding-cuts%2F&via=canberrawkly "Twitter") [WhatsApp](https://api.whatsapp.com/send?text=Larger+classes%2C+less+support%3F+ACT+parents+fear+school+funding+cuts%20%0A%0A%20https://canberradaily.com.au/larger-classes-less-support-act-parents-fear-school-funding-cuts/ "WhatsApp") [Email](mailto:?subject=Larger%20classes,%20less%20support?%20ACT%20parents%20fear%20school%20funding%20cuts&body=https://canberradaily.com.au/larger-classes-less-support-act-parents-fear-school-funding-cuts/ "Email") [Copy URL](https://canberradaily.com.au/larger-classes-less-support-act-parents-fear-school-funding-cuts/ "Copy URL")

Canberra parents fear larger class sizes and reduced learning and disability support under changes to public school funding, as 18 ACT public schools face budgets more than 5 per cent below their projected expenditure this year.

All ACT public schools received their projected budgets and staffing profiles for 2027 on Tuesday, as the ACT Government moves towards what education minister Rachel Stephen-Smith says will be a more equitable funding model.

Compared with schools’ projected expenditure in 2026, 22 schools’ budgets will increase by more than 5 per cent in 2027; 18 face reductions of more than 5 per cent; and 52 will see changes of between minus and plus 5 per cent.

ACT Parents, the peak body representing public school parents and carers, has expressed “strong concerns that the funding will not be enough to respond to the needs in our schools”, executive officer Veronica Elliott said.

![](https://canberradaily.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/VE-photo.jpg) Veronica Elliott, executive officer of ACT Parents. Photo supplied

Ms Elliott said families needed school-specific information about what the changes would mean for their children and why.

“While some schools may experience minimal change, others are preparing for substantial adjustments,” Ms Elliott said. “We have also heard concerns about larger class sizes; reduced learning and disability support; and the continuation of interventions.”

One P&C has written to the Education Directorate’s director-general, concerned that larger class sizes and reduced support could leave its school prioritising immediate safety needs while other students miss out on adjustments and early intervention.

The ACT Government is investing $1.2 billion in public education in 2026-27 – 7.3 per cent more than the previous financial year, Ms Stephen-Smith said. This includes an additional $40.5 million to help schools transition to the new funding model.

The independent ACT Public School System Resourcing Review – [announced in May](https://canberradaily.com.au/generational-shift-for-act-public-schools/) as a ‘generational shift’ towards a coordinated public education system – recommended that staffing above schools’ Student Resource Allocation be redeployed across the public school system to address inequities in resourcing.

Thirteen schools will receive additional funding from an $8 million fund to help them manage staffing, curriculum delivery and complex student needs during the transition.

The government has allocated $25.5 million to support students with disability, including additional funding for all four specialist schools, and $7 million to improve educational outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students.

All four specialist schools will receive more funding next year.

Ms Stephen-Smith acknowledged that “the new approach to school budgets has been challenging for many school communities”.

She said: “The Education Directorate will continue to support school leaders and staff as they work to deliver a great public education for their students.”

Final school budgets will be determined in March or April, once enrolments are known.

While ACT Parents supports equitable funding, Ms Elliott said the Student Resource Allocation methodology must be reviewed, as the Public School System Resourcing Review recommended.

“These budget changes are an early step in reform,” Ms Elliott said. “Their success will be judged by whether resources reach the students and schools that need them, and whether students receive consistent teaching and effective support.”

ACT Parents was concerned that schools might not receive sufficient resources to support students with disability or additional needs, particularly where their needs had not been fully recognised.

“Teachers and school teams need access to specialist expertise to identify needs and provide effective support,” Ms Elliott said. “Without that, students risk missing out on support and schools risk missing out on the funding needed to provide it.”

ACT Parents is already aware of requests or expectations for P&Cs to contribute to school initiatives in 2027. Ms Elliott said that P&Cs were “under no obligation to fund the essentials of public education and doing so can hide the true cost of meeting students’ needs”.

“A student’s access to essential teaching and support should not depend on their community’s fundraising capacity,” Ms Elliott said.

ACT Parents wants the Education Directorate to ensure families receive clear information about changes to classes, staffing, programs and support before the end of the school year; explain how unmet needs will be addressed; and provide pathways for families to raise concerns.

“Students must remain at the centre,” Ms Elliott said. “Finalising budgets cannot mean closing the conversation: arrangements need to be checked regularly in 2027 against what students are actually receiving.”

Both the Canberra Liberals and the ACT Greens have called on the government to identify which schools face funding reductions.

Canberra Liberals education spokeswoman Elizabeth Lee said the announcement vindicated concerns that the Opposition, teachers, parents and school communities had raised for months.

“The Minister can no longer hide behind spin,” Ms Lee said. “If schools are receiving less funding than they did before, that is a cut, regardless of what language the Minister chooses to use.”

Ms Lee called upon Ms Stephen-Smith to release immediately the budgets for every ACT government school, including which schools would receive funding cuts, the size of the cuts, and their effect on staffing levels and programs.

ACT Greens education spokeswoman Laura Nuttall said the government had “left families in the dark” by not identifying the 18 schools facing reductions of more than 5 per cent.

“The Government has suggested that releasing school-specific information would present psychosocial hazards. But what they are completely failing to consider is the psychosocial hazards resulting from the uncertainty and anxiety caused by withholding that information from school communities.

“Students, parents, carers and school staff deserve transparency. The government must now come clean and release school-specific information to parents and guardians across Canberra and make sure schools are genuinely supported as they deal with the Government’s cuts.”

# Ruto says Ksh784B education budget will ease school costs for Kenyan parents

Wednesday 18th November, 2026 04:50 PM\|By [Aloys Michael](https://peopledaily.digital/author/aloys-michael "Posts by Aloys Michael")

![Ruto says Ksh784B education budget will ease school costs for Kenyan parents](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Ruto-2-768x528.png)President William Ruto during the State of the Nationa Address on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. PHOTO/A screengrab by PD Digital/K24TV

President William Ruto has defended increased government spending on education, saying investments in teachers, classrooms and laboratories are intended to reduce the financial burden on parents and make schooling more affordable.

Speaking during his State of the Nation Address to Parliament on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, Ruto said the government had increased the annual education allocation from Ksh521 billion in the 2022/23 financial year to Ksh784 billion in the current financial year.

The President said the additional funding was part of efforts to shift the responsibility of financing essential education services from households to the government, amid concerns over the cost of schooling.

He said parents had previously been forced to contribute towards hiring teachers, constructing classrooms and providing learning facilities in schools across the country.

![Teachers at Kasarani stadium duting the celebrations of World Tewachers Day 2026. PHOTO/Emoo FM](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/tsc-500x333.jpg)Teachers at Kasarani stadium duting the celebrations of World Tewachers Day 2026. PHOTO/Emoo FM

## **100,000 teachers hired as government targets staffing gaps**

Ruto said his administration had made significant progress in addressing the teacher shortage that stood at approximately 116,000 when he took office, noting that the government had recruited 100,000 teachers over the past four years.

He added that another 20,000 teachers were expected to be recruited, a move he said would improve learning conditions and reduce the need for parents to fund teachers hired through school Boards of Management.

“When we assumed office, Kenya faced a teacher shortage estimated at 116,000,” Ruto said.

“In four years, we have employed 100,000 teachers and are preparing to recruit another 20,000.”

The recruitment drive, according to the President, is intended to strengthen teaching capacity in public schools while reducing the financial pressure on households that have been forced to contribute towards staffing costs.

## **23,000 classrooms constructed across the country**

The Head of State also highlighted investments in school infrastructure, saying the government had constructed 23,000 classrooms and was undertaking the construction and equipping of 1,600 laboratories.

He said the infrastructure projects were designed to expand access to learning facilities and ease the financial demands placed on communities to improve schools.

“We have built 23,000 classrooms and are constructing and equipping 1,600 laboratories,” Ruto said.

The President argued that the investments would help reduce the pressure on parents to meet costs associated with essential school infrastructure, while improving the learning environment for pupils and students.

![Teachers Service Commission (TSC) buildings.PHOTO/@TSC_KE/X](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Pg-5-TSC-Building-2025-07-23-at-8.09.57-PM%E2%88%9A-500x283.jpg)Teachers Service Commission (TSC) buildings. PHOTO/@TSC\_KE/X

## **Ruto warns schools against unauthorised charges**

Ruto said the increased education allocation must be properly managed and reach schools on time, warning that parents should not be forced to finance government obligations through unauthorised charges.

He said the objective of increasing public expenditure on education was to make schooling more accessible and affordable while ensuring learners acquire skills that can help them secure employment in the future.

“Our resources must reach schools promptly and be managed responsibly. Parents should not be required to carry public obligations through unauthorised charges,” he said.

The President said education remained a critical investment in household incomes and the country’s economic growth, arguing that keeping children in school and equipping them with practical skills would strengthen families and the nation.

## **3.6 million learners sit national examinations**

Ruto also addressed the ongoing national examinations, saying 3.6 million learners were sitting the Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA), Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA) and Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE).

He described the cohort as the largest in the country’s history and said the examinations had been conducted in a c [alm environment without the tension and heavy security deployments witnessed in previous years](https://peopledaily.digital/news/state-of-the-nation-address-ruto-highlights-local-printing-of-kcse-kjsea-examinations).

“For the first time in 65 years, examination papers were printed here in Kenya,” he said, adding that the examinations had been conducted in an orderly atmosphere.

Ruto said examinations should be treated as a normal part of learning rather than events that instil fear among candidates, insisting that assessments should measure learners’ progress without threatening their future.

He said the government’s education investments were aimed at lowering the cost of schooling, improving access to facilities and preparing learners for productive employment.
